item.title: Where can I watch the Dolphins vs. Patriots game?
item.description: The Miami Dolphins hosting the New England Patriots will be relegated to a very local regional coverage on Sunday afternoon.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins, coming off their first win in 2026, face a second-straight AFC East division rival this weekend. Having dispatched the New York Jets in Week 7, Miami returns to South Florida to host the New England Patriots in a late-afternoon Week 8 contest.

The Dolphins moved to 1-5 on the season with their victory, using their Week 6 bye week to make adjustments and continue the growth of the league’s youngest team and, ultimately, land the first victory for head coach Jeff Hafley. Now they will look to upset the Patriots, who fell to 4-3 this year with a Week 7 Thursday night loss to the Chicago Bears.

The Patriots at Dolphins game is one of only two games in the late-afternoon slot – but the Kansas City Chiefs at Denver Broncos game is nearly a national broadcast with Miami-New England relegated to local networks.

Where will the Patriots vs. Dolphins game air on TV?

The game is on CBS with Andrew Catalon, Logan Ryan, and A.J. Ross on the call. The current plan is for Miami, West Palm Beach, and Fort Myers to pick up the game in Florida, while the New England region, from Connecticut and Rhode Island through Massachusetts, Vermont, and New Hampshire, and across Maine getting the broadcast.

Otherwise, the country will see the Chiefs and Broncos. Broadcast plans can still be adjusted, with local CBS affiliates shifting the game they will air, but for now, it is an extremely limited region for the Dolphins-Patriots contest.

What other games will I see in Florida?

1 p.m. Eastern time slot

CBS will air the Buffalo Bills at Baltimore Ravens game to start the day in South Florida, including Miami, West Palm Beach, and Fort Myers, up through Tampa. The rest of the state, north from Orlando and across the Panhandle, will see the Indianapolis Colts at Jacksonville Jaguars game.

The FOX broadcast plan is more broken across the state. Miami will see the Las Vegas Raiders at New York Jets game. West Palm Beach is slated to see the Minnesota Vikings at Detroit Lions game, while the majority of the rest of the state will have the Atlanta Falcons at Tampa Bay Buccaneers game. Jacksonville will not have a game on FOX to avoid the conflict of the local broadcast on CBS. The western end of the Panhandle will get the Arizona Cardinals at Dallas Cowboys game.

4:05/4:25 p.m. Eastern time slot

We covered the FOX plan for the late slot when discussing the Dolphins game. CBS does not have the doubleheader, this week, but Jacksonville will have the Los Angeles Chargers at Los Angeles Rams game.

8:20 p.m. Eastern time slot – Sunday Night Football

The Sunday Night Football game this weekend will feature the Philadelphia Eagles at Washington Commanders game.

item.title: Fantasy Football Rankings: Hayden Winks' QB, TE, D/ST, kicker Blueprint for Week 8
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Hayden Winks sets the table at the onesie positions for Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
The Blueprint is my weekly column and basically everything that I use to build out the most accurate rankings I can. There will be an RB column, a WR column and a this combination column on the onesie positions. You will find film notes and endless charts. Maybe enough charts to stress test the Yahoo website. I kid.

It's impossible to get every ranking thoroughly early in the week, so be sure to keep checking in on these columns through Sunday morning. As always, my full rankings at every position are available.

Week 8 Projected Points

Week 8 QB Rankings

1. Josh Allen (vs. BAL) - 22.9 proj. points

Allen continues to lead all quarterbacks with 28.1 half PPR points per game as the clear-cut QB1. A combination of being the QB6 in EPA per dropback while also averaging 40.0 rushing yards per game (QB2) makes him a Round 2 value in fantasy. Keep in mind that DJ Moore has barely played this year, too. He should be back for this game.

Week 8 brings a home tilt against a Ravens defense allowing the 19th-most half PPR points per game to QBs. Baltimore just surrendered 28.9 fantasy points and four passing touchdowns to Joe Burrow in Week 7, and that game included downfield shots and some out-of-structure moments. Those are Allen's specialties. Buffalo enters as 3.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 28.5 points (second). Lamar Jackson is also expected to play.

2. Lamar Jackson (at BUF) - 21.4 proj. points

We'll get more confirmation on his status later, but healthy Lamar Jackson was pacing to be the MVP before this ankle sprain. His +0.40 EPA per dropback is the best in the NFL. He isn't rushing the ball like in his prime (36 YPG), but new OC Declan Doyle is adding more explosiveness in the air by unlocking Zay Flowers and sprinkling in Ja'Kobi Lane's catch radius underneath and along the sideline. It's a fun offense when everyone is out there together.

The Bills defense has some nice players but lacks the depth or the experience in this new scheme to be a great unit. They've allowed the third-most fantasy points to QBs (23.5) and the second-most passing yards per game (299), which would be the most in the NFL if it were a QB itself. Lamar Jackson had a 29.4-point game against them in Week 1 of last year and cleared 22.1 points in each of his 2024 contests. Most recently, it was Kirk Cousins (QB8), Matthew Stafford (QB6) and Drake Maye (QB1) popping off.

3. Drake Maye (at MIA) - 21.4 proj. points

Maye enters Week 8 as the QB3 (22.4 PPG) on the season while generating +0.12 EPA per dropback (QB15). Over his last four starts, his efficiency has jumped to +0.41 EPA per dropback (QB1) and 30.2 fantasy points per game. He continues to offer a functional rushing baseline, contributing 30.1 rushing yards per game (sixth). I'm not sure if A.J. Brown is good enough to take Maye over the top to the next tier, but the role players are making enough plays to make him an A-tier QB1 again.

The Patriots now draw a Dolphins defense allowing the seventh-most half PPR points per game to QBs. Miami recently surrendered 24.6 points to Joe Burrow (QB8) and 23.5 points to Geno Smith (QB5) in its last two games. New England is listed as 7.5-point road favorites with an implied team total of 26.0 points (fifth).

4. Dak Prescott (vs. ARI) - 24.9 proj. points

Prescott stalled out from Weeks 3-6 but rebounded last week against the Eagles with a three-score outing. He's the QB15 across the season. That should be his worst stretch, however. The schedule loosens up, and his entire OL is healthy and playing extremely well. They've also doubled down on just throwing to their superstar duo of WRs. It's an awesome environment.

The Cowboys have the highest team total of the week (30.75 points), and that'll be one of the highest of any team all year. Bo Nix (QB3), Jared Goff (QB4) and Jameis Winston (QB6) all had huge outings most recently versus the Cardinals. Arizona's DT1 Walter Nolen has been sidelined, too. It's go time at home.

5. Jayden Daniels (vs. PHI) - 20.9 proj. points

Daniels is the per-game QB7 this year, even including the halftime exit in Week 2. He's rebounded with QB3 and QB7 performances, respectively, since returning from his dislocated elbow, and that brace or the threat of another injury hasn't dissuaded him from rushing like normal. He's the QB1 in rushing yards per game (53.3). His issue is no Terry McLaurin. They did get Chig Okonkwo back and will have explosive third-rounder Antonio Williams to fill the gap, but it's a pretty mediocre skill group for a first-time play caller. Daniels' rushing floor is still far too valuable to have any worry, though.

The upcoming date with Philadelphia presents a test against a defense yielding the eighth-most half PPR points to the position (20.4 per game). Recent opposing QBs have posted solid numbers against the Eagles, including Dak Prescott (23.3 points), Bryce Young (19.8), and Trevor Lawrence (23.7 points). Philadelphia also sits seventh in half PPR points allowed to QB rushing, and its LB/S/CB2 play has been very underwhelming. Last Monday night's loss included poor effort by its superstar DT duo, too. Washington enters this home clash as 4.5-point home favorites with a 23.25-point implied team total (14th). I don't view Philly as a great unit right now.

6. Joe Burrow (vs. TEN) - 24.4 proj. points

Burrow has operated as the per-game QB2 (23.0 PPG) through six games, posting +0.21 EPA per dropback (QB8). He leads the league with 2.5 passing touchdowns per game, throwing multiple touchdowns in four consecutive starts. Cincinnati has leaned into the pass heavily, ranking first in neutral pass rate at 65% on early downs. That volume meets a Titans defense that ranks 22nd in half PPR points allowed to quarterbacks. Tennessee has given up at least 20 fantasy points to opposing signal callers in three of their past four games. The Bengals are 10-point home favorites with an implied team total of 28.25 points (third).

Burrow's downfield shots have been in a league of their own:

Then there are the Titans. It's been a struggle in the secondary all year long with one of their main free agents being healthy-scratched at CB. Deshaun Watson (QB10), Daniel Jones (QB12), CJ Stroud (QB14) and part-time Lamar Jackson (QB11) have all had nice outings against them this month. And they just traded Jeffery Simmons. A large 28.25-point team total (third) for the Bengals is unsurprising.

7. Trevor Lawrence (vs. IND) - 19.9 proj. points

Fresh off the bye, Lawrence is currently the per-game QB11 (20.4 PPG) on the year while generating +0.30 EPA per dropback (QB4). He has thrown 14 touchdown passes across six starts, alongside 11.7 rushing yards per game (20th). He'll be without one of his tackles for the rest of the year, but they at least have one of the most experienced swing tackles behind him. In general, Lawrence has a great coaching staff and skill talent around him, while being behind an iffy OL. That was true last year when he was a fantasy QB1.

Jacksonville now hosts a tanking Indianapolis defense that ranks 12th in half PPR points allowed to QBs. They just traded DT1 DeForest Buckner and the best LG in the NFL in Quenton Nelson this week. Sauce Gardner has also missed time recently. It's arguably the worst defense on paper right now. The Jaguars enter as 7.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 28.25 points (third).

8. Jordan Love (vs. CAR) - 19 proj. points

Love has delivered steady per-game scoring as the QB14 (19.6 half PPR points), averaging 280 passing yards per contest (fourth) with +0.13 EPA per dropback (QB12). He has generated multiple passing scores in six of seven starts, operating comfortably within Green Bay's pass-friendly approach. This team is easily leading in air yards, and even with RB Josh Jacobs back last week, they had an above-average neutral pass rate. That's because their OL is terrible (and on their third-string C now), and they trust Love to figure out the most. Things could change if Matthew Golden (shoulder/foot) can't suit up on Thursday Night Football.

The Panthers can be absolutely gashed on the ground, allowing the most rushing yards per game (153.2). They are also missing their top-two corners and EDGE1 Jaelan Phillips, so it's more than their entire defense stinks than they are a strict run funnel. Jared Goff dropped 412 total yards on them in Week 4 when the Panthers offense was alive. Green Bay carries a 25.5-point implied team total (seventh) as 3.5-point home favorites.

9. Matthew Stafford (vs. LAC) - 19 proj. points

The Rams used 3-TE sets at a league-high rate last game without Davante Adams, and that'll continue to be their plan. It likely means a far lower average depth of target with narrower margins, but they've had tons of success in these heavier looks and are still third in neutral pass rate (63%). Puka Nacua looks like he isn't at 100% either on tape, but that didn't stop Stafford from being the QB11 last week in a blowout win. He's the QB13 in fantasy points per game on QB2 yards, QB6 touchdowns and QB34 rushing.

Now he draws a Chargers defense that is 25th in half PPR points allowed to QBs, surrendering just 13.0 fantasy points per game to QB passing (27th). Some of that is schedule and scheme, but there isn't a talent advantage to me, especially with LB/S Derwin James sidelined. If the Chargers offense can threaten an injured Rams defense at all, it's a good spot for Stafford. Los Angeles enters as 6.5-point home favorites with a 26.0-point team total (fifth).

10. Jacoby Brissett (at DAL) - 19.9 proj. points

Brissett is not creating, nor is he pushing the ball enough to be trusted week to week. That said, Brissett is functional enough to soak up garbage time stats when the opposing defense is leaky. He has been the QB5 against the 49ers and QB7 against the Lions this season, while predictably stinking it up against SEA, LAC, LAR and DEN. The hope is that Jeremiyah Love is back so they can start phasing out the Tyler Allgeier runs, and eventually these 50/50 balls to Michael Wilson will result in big plays instead of incompletions.

This week's matchup against the Cowboys falls into the leaking bucket. And it's overflowing. They've allowed 20.3 fantasy points per game to QBs (ninth) with countless coverage busts in an inexperienced defense that is featuring rookies and a first-time play caller. Offenses have thrown on just 44% of their neutral situations against Dallas (32nd), but the Cardinals likely won't have that luxury here. Jordan Love (QB5) and C.J. Stroud (QB4) lit it up through the air and Jalon Daniels pulled off the upset in Week 5 against them. Arizona heads on the road as 6.5-point road underdogs with an implied total of 24 points (12th).

11. Caleb Williams (at SEA) - 19.9 proj. points

Williams is dicing defenses up from the pocket far more now than he ever has before. Scary. He hasn't needed to run as much since the hamstring injury, but now that we're in the third game back, he can probably start leaning into it more when needed. Williams is the QB5 in EPA per dropback this season and has been fantasy's QB1, QB15 and QB7 in his three games away from the Flores-in-the-rain game. He won't have TE2 Cole Kmet now, but that could mean fewer under center runs in favor of more 3-WR sets that get Luther Burden III onto the field more. Not a bad swap for Williams.

The Seahawks are easily a top-two defense in the NFL. They've allowed just 12.7 fantasy points per game to QBs (31st) on the fewest passing yards per game (158). They are the best rushing defense by a mile as well. If there is a weakness, it's in the secondary at post safety and CB2, and Williams has the skill set to buy time and deliver it that way. It's just a very small window. Just ask Patrick Mahomes (179 scoreless yards) and Bo Nix (109 scoreless yards) most recently. The closer comp is probably Brock Purdy, who was the QB17 with 16.2 fantasy points in Week 5. Chicago heads into Lumen Field as 3-point road underdogs with a 21.75-point team total (18th).

12. Jared Goff (vs. MIN) - 20 proj. points

Goff is quietly the QB4 in fantasy points per game (22.2) on QB3 EPA per dropback and the most passing yards per game (QB1). Their defense has left them in shootouts, and Goff's maturity in the offense speaks for itself. He is the most under-appreciated thrower in the game right now.

Detroit now welcomes a Minnesota defense that is not only the best in just about every pass-game mark this season but is really changing the game defensively across the league. They've allowed 10.3 fantasy points per game to QBs with the most recent starters putting up 5.6, 3.8, and 4.5 fantasy points. That is straight-up hilarious. Now, Goff is much better equipped to handle the pressures DC Brian Flores delivers and has been better under pressure later in his career. The problem is offenses facing Minnesota have passed in neutral situations just 47% of the time (bottom-three), and it's been harder to find explosives too. A minimized 24.75-point team total (ninth) seems fair. This is truly elite offense versus elite defense. Can't wait.

13. Kyler Murray (at DET) - 20.4 proj. points

Murray has to play better. He looks extremely fast (QB9 in rush YPG), but his accuracy on these timing routes has been lacking and he's turned down other intermediate throws. He has made enough splash plays to keep the Vikings undefeated, but it hasn't been a sustainable offense so far. That could change at any point.

Where Kyler Murray can go from here will be one of the biggest stories of the 2026 season. The defense is certified elite. They're on pace for home field advantage. The OL and WR rooms are nice.

If he can play well, they've got it all. pic.twitter.com/TugvRj7Ls9

— Hayden Winks (@HaydenWinks) October 26, 2026

What a matchup for him here. The Lions are allowing the most fantasy points to QBs (27.2) and passing yards per game (313.5). Jordan Love (QB12), Jacoby Brissett (QB7), Bryce Young (QB7) and Geno Smith (QB4) have been electric against them this month, and only Love is firmly better than Murray. Minnesota has been more conservative on offense because its defense is outstanding, but we'll see if they open it up a bit against the Lions. The Vikings have a 21.75-point team total.

14. Kirk Cousins (at NYJ) - 19 proj. points

Cousins has cleared 17.8 fantasy points in 6 of 7 games as the QB12 across the season. The Raiders pass game has been fun while living in 2-TE land, and Tre Tucker is making enough downfield magic happen for Cousins to be treated seriously in the best matchups. It sounds like coach Klint Kubiak wants to see more of Cousins, rather than get Fernando Mendoza reps, so let's ride this while we can. Cousins is the QB13 in EPA per dropback, QB6 in pass yards per game (268) and QB4 in passing touchdowns per game (QB4).

The Jets are pretty soft defensively. They allowed Malik Willis to win his first game on the back of a QB4 overall finish, and Drake Maye was the QB4 as well the week prior, even with A.J. Brown dropping the ball all game long. The Raiders have a solid 22.0-point team total (16th) as slight road underdogs. The Jets offense is good enough to put up points on the Raiders, so this does have some sloppy shootout appeal.

15. Bryce Young (at GB) - 16.5 proj. points

Young caved under pressure last week right away, and when he was in must-drop-back situations, the offense looked stuck. He'll be without star LG Damien Lewis and RT Taylor Moton on a short rest. Young is fantasy's QB8 this season on QB3 passing yards per game and the second-highest neutral pass rate, but he's also been at his best against CHI, ATL, DET and PHI.

The chaos Bucs and Browns have slowed him down, and I'd put the Packers in that bucket based on how they're coached and with the talent they have at safety. Green Bay has allowed the fifth-fewest fantasy points to QBs (15.3) but has struggled against the run at times. They recently kept Jared Goff (QB13) and Dak Prescott (QB17) out of the QB1 podium. Carolina is listed as 3.5-point road underdogs with a 22-point team total (16th).

16. Patrick Mahomes (at DEN) - 19.4 proj. points

Let's see if Rashee Rice and RT Jaylon Moore are going to play first. They'll make a big difference after last week's flop against the Seahawks. The Broncos defense is back to tip-top shape with CB1 Pat Surtain, CB2 Riley Moss and EDGE2 Jonathon Cooper back. Mahomes was the QB9 against the diminished version of the Broncos in Week 1 (207-3 total) but has been the QB13, QB12 and QB29 with 0-1 total touchdowns in his other recent outings against them. Kansas City has a 21.0-point team total, and Mahomes hasn't run it nearly as much as last year to save fantasy days with 11.8 rushing yards per game (QB19).

17. Aaron Rodgers (vs. CLE) - 18 proj. points

18. Sam Darnold (vs. CHI) - 18.4 proj. points

19. Baker Mayfield (vs. ATL) - 19.4 proj. points

20. Malik Willis (vs. NE) - 15.9 proj. points

21. Bo Nix (vs. KC) - 19.4 proj. points

Nix had a wild 60-yard scramble TD and a long RJ Harvey screen TD against a blitz; good to see but can't be relied on moving forward. The bigger takeaway was Nix's aggressiveness as a passer, specifically in empty sets where he had a 16.6 aDOT on five attempts, leading to 94 yards. If Nix isn't comfortable turning his back post-snap, then these types of wrinkles from Sean Payton will help on the margins. It's good to see Denver's pass rate tick back up, too.

Unfortunately, Nix completed just 13 passes on 30 dropbacks outside of those empty looks. That's against the Cardinals!!! The box score was a lot better than the tape to me.

22. Michael Penix Jr. (at TB) - 18.4 proj. points

23. Deshaun Watson (at PIT) - 16.4 proj. points

24. Tanner McKee (at WAS) - 13.4 proj. points

25. Justin Herbert (at LAR) - 19.4 proj. points

26. Geno Smith (vs. LV) - 18.9 proj. points

27. Daniel Jones (at JAX) - 13.9 proj. points

28. Cam Ward (at CIN) - 13.9 proj. points

Week 8 TE Rankings

1. Trey McBride (at DAL) - 69.5 proj. yards

McBride enters as the TE3 on TE1 usage over his last 4 games, averaging 10.8 targets and 16.5 expected half PPR points. He is coming off a season-high 22.1 half PPR points in Week 7, hauling in 10-of-13 targets for 111 yards and 1 touchdown. This is a carbon copy of last year's TE1 overall finish.

Dallas ranks 18th in half PPR points allowed to TEs at 9.8 per game, and they are a little more talented at LB and S than they are CB. By no means is this a difficult spot, and the game script is as favorable as it gets with the Cardinals projected to lose by a touchdown while carrying a 24.0-point team total (12th) themselves. He had 55-1 receiving in a win over the Cowboys last year.

2. Brock Bowers (at NYJ) - 69.5 proj. yards

Bowers is the TE1 on TE2 overall usage this season. It's been a bit quieter in the last two games with star-level DBs covering him in isolation, but Bowers still holds the line in tougher matchups and will dominate the easier ones. Even with a season-low 8 targets in Week 7 (first of all, lol), he secured 6 receptions for 73 yards and a 19% target share. Over the past month he's averaging 103 air yards per game. Incredible.

The Jets sit 27th in half PPR points allowed to TEs (just 8.0 per game), though they did allow double-digit scores to Hunter Henry (12.8) in Week 6 and Greg Dulcich (11.1) in Week 7. There's nothing too scary about their DB room on paper, but their LB room has been solid. The Raiders enter as 1.5-point road underdogs with an implied total of 22 points (17th). This game has sloppy shootout appeal.

3. Tucker Kraft (vs. CAR) - 39.5 proj. yards

After limited snaps and uncharacteristic drops and poor blocking early on, Kraft has rebounded recently. He's the TE10 on TE7 usage over his last 4 games, averaging 6.5 targets and 11.0 expected half PPR points. We haven't seen the signature YAC moments from, but those will come eventually. It sounds like Matthew Golden will play despite missing the short week of practices. Any injury to the top-2 targets would be a big deal, as they have little skill group depth.

Carolina ranks 14th in half PPR points allowed to opposing tight ends at 11.0 per game, having yielded monster weeks to Harold Fannin (20.6) and Sam LaPorta (18.4) earlier this season. They are better at LB and nickel than they are elsewhere right now, but the entire defense is in tough shape. Green Bay is listed as 3.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 25.5 points (6th). His touchdown odds are higher than most, even if he's less likely to see 8+ targets.

4. Colston Loveland (at SEA) - 39.5 proj. yards

Loveland had a trio of explosives detached from the OL; a TD in a 3-TE set where he made a defender miss, an awesome in-breaking where he showed rare route running against a nickel and a fourth-down conversion in man coverage. A few balls off his hands prevented an even bigger day, but long story short: Loveland is back. He's the TE2 and TE5 in expected points, respectively, since Caleb Williams has returned. In games with him since Week 10 last year, Loveland is the TE5 on TE3 usage.

A matchup with the Seahawks is a doozy. They're 3rd-best against fantasy TEs this year on the fewest passing yards per game (158). They have LB/S Nick Emmanwori and LB Ernest Jones roaming the middle of the field, paired with one of the most dominant DLs. The Bears are still projected for 21.75 points (16th) despite the very difficult road matchup, but that is far worse than normal. The margins are thinner for Loveland.

5. Sam LaPorta (vs. MIN) - 49.5 proj. yards

The road is rocky on a week to week basis given the amount of star-level skill players they have, but LaPorta tends to be worth the stomach ache. He's the TE6 on TE4 usage this season with amazing yards after the catch and red zone usage. He can leave games with a 6% target share like he did last week, but he can also finish as the TE1 overall like he did in Week 4. It is what it is.

The Vikings have shut down opposing TEs all season, allowing the fewest half PPR points per game to the position at 5.4 (32nd). Opponents facing Minnesota have leaned heavily away from the pass, posting an extreme 47% neutral pass rate (3rd-lowest), and when teams do pass, they often times keep their TEs in to block. They're also very smart at LB and S, making it harder to find coverage busts. Detroit heads into the divisional matchup as 3-point home favorites with a 24.75-point team total (9th).

6. Tyler Warren (at JAX) - 39.5 proj. yards

We'll see if he can return, but the Jaguars defense is the biggest pass funnel in the NFL this year. It'd be a great spot for him, with their safeties being the weakest link on the team.

Separately, Warren is a great buy low with Josh Downs (and maybe Keenan Allen) being shopped ahead of the deadline. They will be trailing often the rest of the way without Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, and Warren has been an excellent PPR scam before.

7. Brenton Strange (vs. IND) - 39.5 proj. yards

Strange has carved out consistent volume recently, commanding at least 7 targets in 3-straight outings. Across his last 4 games, he sits as the TE12 on TE9 usage, averaging 8.7 half PPR points, 8.7 expected points per contest, and a 22% target share. In an offense this good, that means Strange is more of a low-end TE1 than a TE2.

Indianapolis ranks 13th in half PPR points allowed to TEs at 11.3 points per game. The Colts have shown vulnerability to the position recently, giving up 19.0 half PPR points to Pat Freiermuth in Week 5 and 11.5 points to T.J. Hockenson in Week 7. Their LB room has been terrible, and they just traded away their best player in DeForest Buckner. Jacksonville hosts this divisional clash as 7.5-point home favorites with a healthy implied team total of 28.0 points (4th).

8. Dalton Kincaid (vs. BAL) - 49.5 proj. yards

There isn't a TE with more variance than Kincaid for a million reasons. When smoothing things out, Kincaid is the TE11 on TE17 usage this season, which is eerily similar to where he finished in 2025. Ironically, he's been better in games with D.J. Moore, though that's small sample noise than anything else. He is capable of lucking into touchdowns or creating an explosive in 1-on-1, but he is also only averaging 4.8 targets per game. Kincaid is a boom-bust TE1/2 in normal games.

Baltimore ranks middle of the pack against TEs, yielding 10.3 half PPR points per game (17th). The Ravens have shown vulnerability to top options, allowing a 5-42-1 line to Kyle Pitts (TE8) in Week 5 and two tight end scores in Week 7 to Drew Sample and Mike Gesicki. It's shocking when they have Kyle Hamilton and Roquan Smith with an elite play-calling head coach, but it's hard to call them a great unit right now. Buffalo enters as 3.5-point home favorites with an implied total of 28.5 points (2nd).

9. Kyle Pitts Sr. (at TB) - 39.5 proj. yards

We should officially throw out the two games without Michael Penix Jr.

Pitts is averaging 3.1 more targets per game, and over the past month, Pitts is the TE4 on TE10 usage. He won't run this pure with touchdowns, but he is passing the receiving eye test, particularly on quick out routes. If Penix continues this quick-release offense with TE whisperer Kevin Stefanski, Pitts stands to benefit.

The Buccaneers have been generous to tight ends, giving up 13.4 half PPR points per game (eighth-most). Tampa Bay has allowed top-12 weekly finishes to Tucker Kraft (TE5), Darnell Washington (TE11) and Darren Waller (TE8) over the past month. Atlanta is listed as 2.5-point road underdogs with a 22.0-point team total (15th).

10. Travis Kelce (at DEN) - 49.5 proj. yards

We'll probably look back at the first three weeks of the year when Kelce was literally leading the NFL in yards after catch as the outlier of the season. Over the past month, Kelce is the TE18 on TE20 despite injuries to multiple WRs. On tape, Kelce looks okay, but even more of his production now is slipping out after chip help or four seconds after the play as Patrick Mahomes runs around. That's fun. It's just going to come with far less consistency, especially when Rice is back.

Denver ranks ninth-friendliest against the position, allowing 12.7 half PPR points per game to TEs. The Broncos just yielded a massive 10-111-1 receiving line on 13 targets to Trey McBride (TE2) in Week 7 and conceded a score to George Kittle (TE4) in Week 4. Kelce had 71 yards in Week 1 and was the TE21 and TE3 in 2025 against them. Kansas City enters as 1.5-point road favorites with a 21.5-point team total (20th).

11. T.J. Hockenson (at DET) - 39.5 proj. yards

Hockenson found the end zone from five yards out in Week 7, catching four of five targets for 35 yards and 11.5 half PPR points against Indianapolis. Over his last four games, he is the TE14 on TE11 usage, averaging 8.3 half PPR points and 8.6 expected points per contest. His underlying opportunity has been volatile, swinging from a massive 13-119-0 line on 13 targets in Week 4 (without Justin Jefferson) to just a single seven-yard grab in Week 5. He holds a 20% target share and 5.8 targets per game over that recent four-game sample.

Detroit has been vulnerable to tight ends, ranking first in half PPR points allowed at 24.7 points per game. Over the last four weeks, the Lions have surrendered big games to Kenyon Sadiq (20.0 half PPR points), Trey McBride (17.1), Teagan Quitoriano (14.5!!!!), and Tucker Kraft (12.8). Their return of S Brian Branch should help alleviate this production, however. Minnesota travels to Detroit as 3-point road underdogs with an implied team total of 21.75 points (19th).

12. Dallas Goedert (at WAS)

Goedert is holding onto low-end TE1 life right now, even with Tanner McKee out there. He's been the TE10, TE17 and TE14 in usage since returning from injury, hovering between 7.1 and 10.0 expected half PPR points. McKee is willing to test throws over the middle, and the OL didn't look horrific last week, to their credit. Goedert's value is highest with DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks sidelined.

Washington represents an elite on-paper spot, ranking second in half PPR points allowed to tight ends (18.4 per game) while offenses throw against them at the second-highest neutral rate in the NFL (60%). They crowd the line of scrimmage and have allowed TEs to leak behind them for a chunk of the year, even with first-round LB Sonny Styles looking like a future All-Pro. Goedert was included in that when he finished as the TE2 overall on 77-2 receiving. The issue is Philadelphia is listed as 4.5-point road underdogs with an implied team total of 18 points (28th). Uh oh.

13. Hunter Henry (at MIA) - 39.5 proj. yards

Henry is the TE7 on TE13 usage across his last 4 games, averaging 11.0 half PPR points on 7.7 expected points per contest. He set season highs with 7 targets, 7 catches, and 71 yards in Week 7, earning a 24% target share in the process. That extended a steady run where he found the end zone in both Week 5 and Week 6 while commanding at least 4 targets in 4 consecutive outings. The fact that A.J. Brown isn't looking like an All Pro player any more paired with the losses of Romeo Doubs and Mack Hollins has led to more reliance on their TE duo. By the way, Eli Raridon is a dude in the making.

Miami has been one of the most vulnerable matchups in the league for tight ends, allowing the 3rd-most half PPR points per game at 17.5. The Dolphins recently allowed a 5-62-2 performance to Mason Taylor (TE1) in Week 7 and a monster 13-119-0 line to T.J. Hockenson (TE2) in Week 4. Travis Kelce and George Kittle taunted them to open the year, too. New England heads on the road as 7.5-point road favorites with a 26.0-point implied total (5th). They'll take advantage of the most inexperienced defense in the league.

14. Chig Okonkwo (vs. PHI) - 24.5 proj. yards

Okonkwo set season highs across the board in Week 6 against San Francisco, hauling in all 7 of his targets for 69 yards and 10.4 half PPR points. That obviously isn't a coincidence with Terry McLaurin leaving that game early. Even in Week 5, Okonkwo was the TE15 on TE20 as he's inched closer to fantasy relevance after an injury derailed his first month. The Commanders have had great fantasy production whenever Jayden Daniels has been healthy, dating back to the Zach Ertz era. There's waiver wire start appeal.

The Eagles rank 26th in half PPR points allowed to TEs, giving up just 8.2 points per game. In their Week 1 meeting, Okonkwo was held to 2 catches for 16 yards on 3 targets, though Tommy Tremble did manage 2 touchdowns against Philadelphia in Week 6 and Brenton Strange posted 68 yards the week prior. I'm less scared of SCB Cooper DeJean and this highly-invested LB room now than I was entering the season. Washington enters as 4.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 22.5 points (14th).

15. Tyler Higbee (vs. LAC) - 24.5 proj. yards

Higbee has settled back into a low-volume role, ranking as the TE21 on TE22 usage over his last four games. After generating 67 and 83 receiving yards in Weeks four and five, his opportunities slipped to four and three targets over his past two outings. He has averaged 46.5 receiving yards and 6.1 half PPR points per game across this four-game stretch, finishing with a modest 11% target share in Week 7. The Rams continue to funnel passes heavily toward their wide receivers, leaving Higbee with minimal underneath work.

Weekly personnel usage:

Rams moving into more heavy-TE usage without Davante Adams pic.twitter.com/nxiqUWCLCd

— Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) October 27, 2026

The upcoming matchup brings a stingy test against the Chargers, who rank 24th in half PPR points allowed to tight ends at 8.8 per game. Los Angeles holds a top-three neutral pass rate at 63% through seven weeks, which gives the passing offense steady baseline dropbacks even in neutral scripts. The Chargers have suppressed tight end rooms consistently, with Dalton Kincaid held to 2.8 half PPR points in Week 3 and Travis Kelce managing 7.3 points in Week 6. The Rams enter as 6.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 25.5 points (seventh).

16. Mark Andrews (at BUF) - 24.5 proj. yards

17. Harold Fannin Jr. (at PIT) - 39.5 proj. yards

Hey! Fannin got his first screen target of the season, obviously resulting in two missed tackles and a first down. He was throwing Titans off himself for much of the game, finishing as the TE14 on TE9 usage after two duds leading into that outing. At the same time, he won't be left wide open for 36-yard gains like he was in this one very often.

Fannin is fighting the breakouts of rookies KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston, so he's only been the TE17 on TE18 usage this year as the most volatile player at his position. Deshaun Watson is missing just enough throws to rule out the upside case, while making enough plays to keep TE1/2 border hope alive.

18. Pat Freiermuth (vs. CLE) - 24.5 proj. yards

19. Colby Parkinson (vs. LAC) - 24.5 proj. yards

Parkinson is a red-zone and check-and-release merchant with rare size (6'7", 266lbs), but it's a role that's needed with the Rams setting a season-high 35 snaps with three+ TEs on the field. He's their best blocker and will be in this role, even if Terrance Ferguson (ankle) returns soon. Tyler Higbee, Dennis Allen and T-Ferg will run fancier routes and are less likely to volleyball-set a target for an INT like Parkinson did last week, but Parkinson can run pure with TDs at any time. He was the TE10 on TE10 usage in Week 6 before last week's TE17 on TE18 usage outing.

Wide receiver Josh Downs has reportedly requested a trade and has garnered interest around the league, but head coach Shane Steichen confirmed Wednesday that Jonathan Taylor — the one everyone, especially fantasy football managers, has their eyes on — has not requested a trade.

Lamar Jackson returning in Week 8?

The Baltimore Ravens are expected to get quarterback Lamar Jackson back for Sunday's matchup against the Buffalo Bills, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and Matt Zenitz of CBS Sports.

Jackson has missed the Ravens' past three games after suffering a high ankle sprain against the Tennessee Titans in Week 4. The quarterback returned to practice last week in a limited capacity before being ruled out for their Week 7 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals.

item.title: Chiefs-Broncos is just one of the pivotal AFC matchups in Week 8
item.description: The conference standings could solidify or be thrown out of whack in Week 8, especially in Kansas City’s matchup.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 8, the Kansas City Chiefs will face the Denver Broncos in a crucial game in the AFC West race. The Chiefs could hold a three-game lead in the division race by sweeping the season series with Denver, while a loss could even out the standings going into the second half of the schedule.

The game kicks off at 3:25 p.m. on Sunday, and it’s just one of the crucial matchups in the AFC playoff race this week.

  • The (5-1) Buffalo Bills will host the (4-3) Baltimore Ravens at Noon
  • The (5-2) Pittsburgh Steelers will host the (5-2) Cleveland Browns at Noon

The Bills lead the AFC East and are the No. 2 seed in the AFC playoff race behind the Chiefs; Kansas City currently holds the tiebreaker because the Bills have one conference loss. The two will match up on Thanksgiving night in Week 12.

The Ravens are currently on the outside looking in, but a win against Buffalo could vault them back into the mix, especially with one of their AFC North foes bound to lose in the other highlighted game.

Cleveland has already beaten Pittsburgh this year and is currently the No. 3 seed in the AFC. So, similar to the Chiefs-Broncos matchup, that game could swing a division race

According to football data analyst Computer Cowboy on X, the Steelers, Ravens and Broncos have a shot to swing their playoff probabilities in the right direction with a victory.

On the flip side, the Chiefs’ AFC West title probabilities could swing from 38% with a loss to 84% with a victory.

A Week 8 win would boost both Buffalo and Kansas City’s chances of earning the No. 1 seed and a postseason bye week.

This weekend, at roughly the year’s midseason point, there is a lot to learn about the contenders in the AFC

item.title: Week 8 game preview: Chicago Bears vs. Seattle Seahawks
item.description: A matchup worthy of Monday Night Football. @SamHouseholder previews Bears-Seahawks
item.content:encoded:
Good teams play in big games and the Chicago Bears have a big game this week. They hit road to play the Super Bowl-champion Seattle Seahawks.

And they’ll do it with a brand new All-Pro defensive tackle! Jeffery Simmons is a Bear!

The Bears are proving themselves to be one of the best offenses in the league with one of the best rising-star quarterbacks.

And their head coach and quarterback face a huge test against one of the league’s best defenses.

Chicago didn’t fare so well in their first defensive test of the year, against the Minnesota Vikings. However, the weather was a factor in that game, like it or not. Plus, Caleb Williams didn’t finish the game. Excuses, maybe, but also realities.

This matchup has a lot of great storylines and will be a measuring stick for the Bears to see how they compete against the league’s best.

It feels like a game with playoff implications. It feels like a game worthy of the Monday Night Football spotlight. It will be the first game in November for the Bears, too. When teams really start to separate themselves.

Let’s meet the Seahawks.

Seattle Seahawks

SB Nation site: Field Gulls

Record: 4-3, second in the NFC West

Last week: 20-3 win over the Kansas City Chiefs

Game day, time, TV: Monday, 7:15 p.m. CT, ESPN

Spread: Seattle -3.5

Bears all-time record against: 8-12, including 2-0 postseason

Historical meeting: The Bears have never beaten the Seahawks in the month of November.

In the second-ever meeting between the teams, the Seahawks beat the Bears 31-29 in week 10 of 1978.

The Bears fell behind 21-9 with Jim Zorn hitting Steve Largent twice for touchdowns and Sherman Smith rushing for another.

But Chicago made a strong comeback.

Roland Harper scored on a 20-yard pass from Mike Phipps. After another Smith touchdown, Walter Payton scored from 7 yards out, drawing the Bears within six. 

The Seahawks drove down the field and tacked on another field goal to go up 31-22.

Phipps threw a pick but Sam McCullum intercepted Zorn right back.

Phipps put together a good drive and Harper scored a 2-yard TD with 40 seconds left.

The Bears managed to recover the onside kick but with 12 seconds left, from Seattle’s 46-yard line, Phipps’ pass was intercepted to end the game.

Last meeting: Who could forget the awful, terrible 6-3 Thursday Night Football game?

Thomas Brown was coaching the Bears. It was a defensive slugfest. Or a total offensive mess. Depends on how you remember it.

The most memorable play didn’t count, as Caleb Williams rolled out and threw an off-platform pass to Rome Odunze four a touchdown. It was called back for offensive holding. (I cannot find a clip online, but I remember it was awesome).

Offense: The Seahawks offense ranks 13th in points and 15th in yards.

Their passing offense is 16th and their rushing offense ranks 17th.

Sam Darnold (62.1 pct. cmp./1,290 yds./8 TD/8 INT) currently leads the league in interceptions, but played a lot better last week.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you likely know about Jaxon Smith-Njigba (58 rec./867 yds./8 TD). Beyond him are AJ Barner (19/180/0), Cooper Kupp (18/199/1), deep threat Rashid Shaheed (16/163/0) and George Holani (12/88/0).

Jadarian Price (28 att./119 yds./0 TD) is injured, but expected to return to practice this week along with Zach Charbonnett (no stats in 2026 yet). In their absence, it’s been Emanuel Wilson (111 att./403 yds./3 TD) and Holani (26/108/1).

Defense: Seattle’s defense comes into Monday night as one the league’s best. They rank fourth in points allowed and first in yards allowed.

Their passing defense ranks first in passing yards and sixth in rushing.

The loaded unit stars Nick Emmanwori (27 tkls/3 TFL/2 sk/1 PD/7 QB hits), DTs Leonard Williams (3 sk/7 TFL/9 QB hits/1 PD), Byron Murphy (3 sk/ 24 tkls/5 TFL/6 QB hits) Derick Hall (3 sk/19 QB hits/3 TFL/1 FF/1 FR) and Ernest Jones (3 sk/68 tkls/3 TFL/2 QB hits/1 INT/3 PD) and Devon Witherspoon (41 tkls/3 PD/3 TFL/1 QB hits)

Other playmakers are Julian Love (2 INT/6 PD/24 tkls/2 TFL), Nehemiah Pritchett (13 tkls/4 PD/2 INT) and Josh Jobe (27 tkls/1 PD/1 INT/1 TFL).

Key matchups: This is a top offense against a top defense. The Bears are going to have to play disciplined football. Take what their given, take shots when they can, use play-action to suck in the LBs. 

On defense, stop JSN. That’s no easy task. The Seahawks can find a running game if Price and/or Charbonnett are back. Anyway to get pressure on Sam Darnold is good though; we know what happens when he is pressured.

Key stats

  • The Seahawks haven’t allowed a 300-yard passer this season. The Rams are the only team with more than 300 passing yards against Seattle since week 2 of last season.
  • Seattle has lost only three times at home going back to the beginning of last season. The 49ers are the only team to beat Seattle at home during this span
  • Despite their strong numbers, the Seahawks have allowed opponents to score on 78.6 percent of their trips inside of the red zone.
  • The Seahawks’ 13 offensive turnovers on the season rank fourth-most in the league. Their 12 defensive turnovers rank third-most.
  • Seattle is allowing a league-low 144.4 passing yards per game and the second-worst passer rating of 72.6. Only the Vikings allow a worse QB rating

Can the Bears hang with a team as good as the Seahawks? How will their offense and QB measure up against Seattle’s defense?

item.title: What to know about Falcons – Buccaneers in Week 8
item.description: The Bucs are gettable, but the Falcons have to come to play against a tough defense.
item.content:encoded:
It’s back to the division for the Falcons, who play the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for the first time in 2026. They’ve lost to the Panthers and beaten the Saints already, but a win here gets Atlanta to 4-4 and puts the hapless Bucs down at 2-6, a hole that will be tough for them to climb out of even in the dismal NFC South. That would be a good time.

The question is whether the Falcons will. The Bucs have been finding their footing a bit, with two wins and one overtime loss in the last three weeks against the Cowboys, Steelers, and Panthers. The Tampa Bay defense is rounding into form as an aggressive, problem-causing unit, dragging a poor offense behind them. If Tampa can force multiple turnovers and get the ground game going, they have a genuine shot in this one. If not, the Falcons could give us a very fun afternoon.

Here’s what you need to know about the game ahead.

Team rankings

On paper, the Buccaneers are not really that much worse than Atlanta. Their passing game is abysmal, but the defense has been good and improving quickly, they run the ball well, and they’ve forced plenty of turnovers. I wouldn’t say Tampa Bay is good, but if they can drag their passing game up to passable, they’ll probably hang around in the division.

Atlanta, meanwhile, is better than its numbers but also inconsistent enough that those numbers can seem like a true reflection of where they’re at. The passing game is league average at worst, the ground game is effective, and the defense has been solid much of the season. It’s just about finding a way to string together quality performances of the caliber they managed against Green Bay, New Orleans, and San Francisco.

How the Bucs have changed in 2026

A fateful decision this offseason was the hiring of Zac Robinson to run the offense after he flamed out in Atlanta. Robinson knows how to put together a compelling run game and has gotten a lot out of Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell, but the passing attack has utterly cratered with Baker Mayfield, injured Baker Mayfield, and rookie Jalon Daniels. You can’t put all of their failures on Robinson, but our criticisms of his passing attacks are carrying over to Tampa Bay.

The Bucs went shopping for Alex Anzalone at linebacker, A’Shawn Robinson for their defensive line, Al-Quadin Muhammad off the edge, and…well, not much else. It was a fairly quiet offseason with an emphasis on defense, which was a little striking after they lost Mike Evans. They also invested their first two picks in the defense, adding linebacker Josiah Trotter and edge Rueben Bain Jr., with promising receiver Ted Hurst their only major addition on offense. This was a team that believed it had outsized defensive needs but a stable offense; that’s not how things have really worked out.

Critically, Tampa Bay also caved and gave Baker Mayfield a contract extension just in time for him to turn into a pumpkin. Mayfield’s numbers were still quite solid but took a nosedive in 2025, and now he’s been either injured or a shadow of himself. You hate to see it*.

*I do not, in fact, hate to see it.

What to know about Week 8

This is a classic letdown matchup that the Falcons must be cautious of. You have a divisional rival that has struggled to this point, but divisional matchups are always a little crazy. The Falcons are riding high after knocking off the undefeated 49ers, but so is Tampa Bay, which dominated Carolina despite a complete lack of a functional passing attack. That should make Atlanta wary and likely will.

We’ll start with the obvious caveat: The Buccaneers have not been able to pass in 2026. Mayfield has started four games and has labored in nearly all of them, throwing for just three touchdowns and two interceptions, absorbing 13 sacks, and playing poorly under pressure, with a measly 4.6 yards per attempt average when the heat is close by. Last week in his return from injury, he threw the ball just 11 times for 64 yards, and his mobility seems to be limited as he’s recovering. There’s talent here—Emeka Egbuka, Chris Godwin, and Cade Otten among them—but Otten’s been quiet, Egbuka has not quite emerged as a difference-making talent, and Godwin is now 30 and has slowed somewhat. Mike Evans is gone, and predictably, the loss of a future Hall of Famer and ageless wonder has indeed slowed this group.

Even if Mayfield and company bounce back somewhat, this is a more pedestrian group than many of the offenses Atlanta has faced. The bigger danger is on the ground, where Bucky Irving and (to a much lesser extent) Kenneth Gainwell have been superb. Irving is a dangerous, slashing runner who is thriving in Robinson’s scheme, and the Falcons have struggled in two of the past three weeks to contain capable runners in Christian McCaffrey and Derrick Henry. They’ll want to make the Bucs one dimensional by getting an early lead and shutting down Irving in the first two quarters, but that’s easier said than done.

Presuming there are no colossal screwups from a defense that largely impressed against a much better team, the Falcons should be able to hold the Bucs to 20 or fewer points. The question concerns whether their offense will be up to the task of overcoming a Bucs defense that very quietly has only allowed more than 17 points once in the past month, has held opposing passing games under 250 yards in all but one game, and has only allowed one team to rush for more than 100 yards against them. Most concerning is the habit of creating turnovers, as the Bucs have eight in their past three games and an ability to create pressure, something Michael Penix Jr. has struggled with more than just about any other quarterback in the NFL.

Compounding the problem is the fact that Bijan has consistently struggled to get going against the Bucs run defense, with his career high of 93 yards against them coming late last year and no other games above 63 yards. The Falcons survived a pedestrian day from Bijan (by his lofty standards, at least) against the 49ers, but if the Bucs can get that done again and impact Penix, it could be a long afternoon for this offense.

The formula is simple enough: Force Mayfield to beat you by bottling up Irving, keep Penix clean and in rhythm, and don’t become one-dimensional. This is a very winnable game against a diminished team, but the Falcons have stumbled many times in the recent past coming off a big win against an inferior opponent. It’s time to buck the trend.

item.title: Indiana’s Omar Cooper Jr. earns back-to-back NFL Rookie of the Week awards
item.description: Cooper Jr. continued his emergence for the Jets this past Sunday, earning yet another weekly award for his efforts.
item.content:encoded:

Former Indiana football wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. was named the Pepsi Rookie of the week following his standout performance against the Miami Dolphins this past Sunday, per an official release from the New York Jets.

Cooper Jr. finished with five receptions for 115 yards and a touchdown against the Dolphins. This just a week after he finished with six receptions for 103 yards and a touchdown against the New England Patrios in his first Rookie of the Week-winning effort.

He’s just the eighth player since the AFL-NFL merger to finish with multiple performances of 100 or more receiving yards in his first three career games and the first to do for for the Jets. Plenty of that production came after the catch, something he got plenty of tape on from his time at Indiana. Notably, the lone game he hasn’t finished with 100 or more receiving yards was his first, which he left early due to injury.

item.title: Bengals on pace for greatest differential of sacks allowed vs. defensive sacks in franchise history
item.description: A stunning stat that shows how much the trenches have been improved.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals had a real problem with both the pass rush and protecting Joe Burrow.

Then they added Amarius Mims, Dylan Fairchild, and Dalton Risner to the line in 2024 and 2025.

And then this past offseason, they went out and got Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe, and Cashius Howell.

The result is a stunning turnaround.

As of right now, they are on pace for the greatest differential between sacks allowed and defensive sacks since sacks were first tracked in 1982.

Currently, the Bengals have a +11 differential (Burrow has been sacked 10 times, while the defense has made 21 sacks), which puts them on pace to be +31 by season’s end.

To put into perspective how far they’ve come, in 2020, the year Burrow was drafted, the Bengals were -31. You read that right.

That’s the second-worst year recorded for the franchise, after 2008, when they were -34.

They’ve been negative every year they’ve had Burrow, but started to improve last year, when they were only -1.

You can see the gradual progress by looking at their ranking of sacks allowed and defensive sacks per year in the Burrow era:

2020 – 28th and 32nd

2021 – 30th and 12th

2022 – 22nd and 29th

2023 – 25th and 18th

2024 – 22nd and 26th

2025 – 14th and 23rd

2026 – 5th and 1st

item.title: Grading the trade: Bears closer to a Super Bowl with Simmons, but the cost was steep
item.description: The Bears added a scheme wrecker who could significantly upgrade their defensive front. The Titans added significant draft resources.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears swung the biggest pre-deadline trade yet by acquiring Titans defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons.

The Bears reportedly will send first-round picks in 2027 and 2028, along with a fourth-round pick in 2027, to the Tennessee Titans for Simmons and a 2028 fifth-rounder.

Simmons, 29, is a four-time Pro Bowl selection and is coming off a first-team All-Pro season in 2025, earning him a three-year, $105.8 million extension in the offseason.

This deal significantly alters the paths for both franchises in the short and long terms. Who got the better end of the trade? Let’s dive into the details.

Bears take big swing for the fences, but at a high cost

The Bears appeared serious about upgrading their talent level prior to the trade deadline, with reported interest in the Colts’ DeForest Buckner prior to him being traded to the 49ers. With the Simmons deal, the Bears made an even bigger plunge – and the price tag reflected that.

By sending their next two first-round picks and a fourth-rounder next year, the Bears are shipping out major assets the next two years. This trade sends a clear signal that the Bears are going for it all this season.  

Simmons remains in the peak of his career, having just turned 29 at the start of training camp, and should have several peak years remaining. He’s played a whopping 425 of the Titans’ 490 defensive snaps (86.7%), which is just about as high a percentage as you’ll see for an interior player. 

The Titans used him as a one-gap penetrator but is capable of lining up at just about any technique up front. He’s a high-motor rusher and an elite run stopper who still demands and draws double teams at a high rate. In his Week 6 game against the Colts, Simmons faced multiple blockers often yet finished with a game-high seven pressures.

This should be a huge addition for Dennis Allen’s front, which has been undermanned. Grady Jarrett, Neville Gallimore and Kentavius Street have taken the majority of the interior snaps, with rookie Jordan van den Berg also filling in. The results have been mediocre. 

The Bears’ defensive rankings might look impressive on the surface (eighth in yards allowed, 10th in points), but on a per-play basis, they’re ranked close to the bottom in several categories. What has saved them is an offense that’s possessing the ball for an average of 35:30 – more than three minutes per game ahead of the next-closest team.

Chicago’s schedule is brutal down the stretch, and they’re going to face some impressive offenses, including two games left vs. the Lions, plus tough tests against the Jaguars, Bills and others. Simmons and some other defensive reinforcements might be enough to stabilize things up front.

The Bears recently got Montez Sweat back from suspension, and he’ll certainly benefit from Simmons’ arrival. It’s a significant stretch for Sweat, who has a major cap hit next season and must finish strong to prove his value. The team also got Shemar Turner back recently and figures to get Dayo Odeyingbo back eventually. With a full cast, this line could turn from a below-average group on the whole to a possible team strength.

Value-wise, this is pretty close to as much compensation as you’ll see moved for a defensive player. But if the Bears make a Super Bowl run, the price very well could make the move a smart one.

Grade: B

Titans gain terrific draft value for Simmons

It’s never easy to deal away an elite talent such as Simmons, especially for a team like Tennessee, which has only so many high-value players. There’s a reason the Titans paid him handsomely in the offseason: Simmons is an elite-level defender coming off a career year.

He’s also played well amid the Titans’ struggles this season, in spite of extra blocking attention on many snaps. Offenses came into most games against them with a plan for Simmons. Now that Titans are losing that, which has to be a blow to defensive-minded head coach Robert Saleh.

But assuming Saleh is back next season, the Titans will have vast resources to use on upgrading the roster. They’re 1-6 and headed toward a top-10 (and likely top-five pick next spring). The Bears pick is expected to be lower, likely in the bottom third of Round 1, but they will now have six choices in the first four rounds and ample flexibility to target whatever they want.

With Cam Ward off to another uneven start, that could even include quarterback – this season or next. Landing the 2028 first-rounder as well gives the Titans a two-years window with major assets to protect themselves in case Ward isn’t the QB they thought he was when they drafted him first overall. If he does pan out, those picks can obviously be allocated to other spots, including to a defense that just lost a major enforcer.

It likely would have been too hard for GM Mike Borgonzi to turn down this offer. He likely had multiple teams bidding and was able to get the Bears up to the price level they were comfortable with. Adding a fourth-rounder in 2027 for a 2028 fifth was a nice little sweetener on top.

The Titans are facing a multi-year rebuild, and this was the best way to help starting towards that effort. They have more needs today than they did yesterday, and picks are merely lottery tickets, but this felt like a deal Borgonzi had to make.

Grade: A-

item.title: Eagles News: Jalen Carter says he’s not playing “to what the fans want, even though it don’t really matter what they want”
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 10/29/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Jalen Carter spoke to reporters on Wednesday after previously declining to answer questions after Monday night’s loss to the Dallas Cowboys. Wasn’t a great look for him to dodge the media after a no-show performance by the defense. Carter clearly isn’t a “trash” player but he’s certainly not living up to the expectations that come with being the highest-paid interior defensive lineman in the NFL. It’s not hard to understand how he could be frustrated, especially while playing through a hairline fracture in his wrist. But I’m not sure including this line about fan expectations is very productive.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

What will it take for Jalen Carter to dominate more consistently? – NBCSP

How does Carter think he’s playing? “I think ya’ll ask me this every year and I say trash,” Carter said. “So trash. I think you asked me this last year and the year before and I gave you the same answer. So trash. Not to my expectations and I guess not to what the fans want, even though it don’t really matter what they want.” Carter isn’t trash, obviously. No one thinks that. He’s a great young talent who needs to turn into a consistently great player.

The Eagles’ lousy season has been full of what-ifs. Let’s answer some of them. – Inquirer

What if the Eagles hadn’t extended Jalen Carter’s contract before this season? In July, the Eagles made Carter the highest-paid defensive tackle in the NFL, handing him a four-year deal worth as much as $160 million. Much was made of how long it took the two sides to reach this agreement — it was announced within 24 hours of the start of training camp — but in reality, the Eagles signed Carter as soon as they could. He was eligible for a new contract after his third NFL season, and he had finished his third NFL season. Now, Carter is so talented — and the Eagles invested so much in him, trading up to draft him with the No. 9 overall pick in 2023 — that one could make a good case that they had no choice but to sign him. They weren’t going to let him walk away in free agency in a couple of years, and if he had an outstanding 2026, it would have been only more expensive to sign him. But aside from one game, that 19-17 loss to Jacksonville in London on Oct. 11, he has not been outstanding, and through his first three seasons, he has been genuinely great for, what, a season-and-a-half? For the first nine weeks of 2023 and all of 2024? What’s more, from his spitting incident last season to his refusal to take public accountability for his and the defense’s subpar performances this season, he has shown few signs if any that he’s maturing into the on-field game-wrecker and off-field leader the Eagles need him to be. Had the Eagles waited to give him the extension, if he were still playing now on his rookie contract, would they be getting a better, more motivated Carter? If they had been more patient, might they have reconsidered letting Milton Williams — who in New England has been every bit as good as Carter, if not better — sign elsewhere?

Commanders cornerback guarantees Washington will beat the Eagles in Week 8 – BGN

Well, if it’s bulletin-board material that will help the Philadelphia Eagles win a football game to snap their five-game losing streak, the Washington Commanders just gave them some. Speaking after practice on Wednesday, Commanders cornerback Amik Robertson guaranteed that his team will beat the Eagles.

Ten hypothetical NFL trade deadline deals that could swing the Super Bowl race – The Athletic

4) DT Moro Ojomo to the Bills. Compensation: Third-round pick. After missing out on Buckner, the Bills could make a splash for a young defensive tackle with loads of potential. Last season, when Ojomo started nine games, he finished with six sacks. He’s just 25, and he could be even more effective in a system like Jim Leonhard’s that gives him freedom to get upfield more often. The Eagles already gave Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter big extensions, so they likely would let Ojomo walk after the season. With their season falling apart, the wise move would be to trade Ojomo, who could be a game-changer for the Bills as a run stuffer and interior pass rusher. He also fits into Buffalo’s 3-4 scheme. Pairing Ojomo with budding star Deone Walker would be a move for this season and the future.

    NFL QB rankings, Week 8: Joe Burrow, Caleb Williams hit season high; Patrick Mahomes slides – NFL.com

    25) Tanner McKee found some success early against the Cowboys’ leaky defense on Monday night, but he couldn’t sustain the production long enough to keep up with the Dallas offense. It’s still clear he’s an inexperienced backup, but he’s playing with an injury-ravaged cast that lowers the ceiling for the entire offense.

    The Longest Autumn – PHLY Eagles

    I know Howie Roseman understands what needs to happen to this roster. This is an organization facing difficult decisions, and those decisions have to be made. But the fascinating question now isn’t simply who stays and who goes. It’s how we find meaning in the rest of this season? How do we remain invested when the stakes that once consumed our Sundays are suddenly gone? Because I don’t want to give up football in October. I don’t want to spend the next three months pretending to care about the gutters. I want to care about the Birds. And today, that’s what we’re going to figure out. How do you survive the longest autumn?

    NFL Told Saquon Barkley to Divest Polymarket Stake – Front Office Sports

    Saquon Barkley was forced to divest his equity stake in Polymarket because NFL players are not allowed to invest in or endorse gambling or prediction-market companies under league rules, the Eagles running back told Front Office Sports. A profile of Barkley revealed last September that Polymarket was among his start-up investments. But at some point between then and this past summer, the league told players they are not allowed to have financial interests in prediction-market platforms. “I am not in that right now,” Barkley told FOS. “I am not allowed to be in that.”

    How will the Giants resolve their quarterback ‘problem’ if J.J. McCarthy continues to play well? – Big Blue View

    The question is: Which quarterback is better, and what should the Giants do with the one who is not the answer to that question? Originally I thought there was a chance the Giants might flip McCarthy to a contending team in the other conference before the trade deadline (which is two days after the Giants’ next game, in Philadelphia). Now I can’t imagine that happening unless McCarthy and the Giants lay such a big egg in Philly that it changes the team’s view of him.

    Flaws and flash carry the Cowboys past the Eagles – Blogging The Boys

    The Dallas Cowboys delivered a performance against the Philadelphia Eagles that was both encouraging and concerning, showcasing their offensive potential and their lingering bad habits on defense. While a 17-point win over a bitter divisional rival is always pleasing, a closer look at the film shows a team still trying to completely put it all together. Let’s highlight some specific elements that jumped out at us after further review.

    Washington Commanders vs. Eagles on SNF Week 8: Inside the Matchup – Hogs Haven

    Unfortunately for Quinn and the Commanders, the Eagles’ weaknesses mirror their own. While Philadelphia’s defense ranks 31st with a 28.7% pressure rate, the Commanders’ offensive line is allowing pressure 39.9% of the time. Similarly, while the Eagles offensive line is allowing pressure with a 41.7% rate, Washington’s defense ranks 17th in pressures with a 34.4% pressure rate and each defense has been extremely poor at generating quick pressures. Both teams have been bad in the trenches, but something will have to give on Sunday night.

    Jeffrey Simmons trade grades for Bears-Titans blockbuster for massive haul of picks – SB Nation

    The Chicago Bears cemented their playoff run on Thursday by landing one of the NFL’s best defensive tackles, sending a massive haul to the Tennessee Titans for All-Pro Jeffrey Simmons. Chicago is sending two first-round picks, and a fourth-round pick to Tennessee to Simmons — who will immediately revamp a defensive line that was in dire need of interior pressure. The Bears also got a 2028 fifth round pick back in the deal, per Adam Schefter. It’s a major investment for the Bears, a sign that the Titans need to rebuild on defense, and the success of this team hinges on what Chicago is able to achieve in the next three-to-four years.

item.title: The biggest benefit for the 49ers from the DeForest Buckner trade
item.description: DeForest Buckner should help the Niners in one big area.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers made a splash this week with the trade for Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, six years after the two sides made the same move back in 2020.

Buckner, now 32, is still a productive defensive tackle, having 31 tackles, 20 pressures, and four sacks this year. Buckner is three years removed from his last Pro Bowl, but he’s already matched his sack total from a season ago and has been healthy this year, giving the 49ers depth.

Immediately, the thought is that the 49ers can pair Buckner and Osa Odighizuwa together, giving San Francisco two quality veteran interior pass rushers. But could this deal actually help both players in a different way?

Through seven games, Buckner has the fourth-highest snap count among defensive tackles at 353. Only Jeffery Simmons (435 snaps), Jalen Carter (419 snaps), and Alim McNeill (363 snaps) have played more. Buckner has been on the field for 82 percent of Indianapolis’s defensive snaps, which would be the second-highest share of his career after his rookie season.

Who’s fifth on that list? Osa Odighizuwa, who has 346 snaps in seven games. Odighizuwa has played in 74 percent of the 49ers defensive snaps, also the second-highest rate of his career.

With a ton of younger players in the rotation, the 49ers have leaned on Odighizuwa a ton to be available this season. He’s still posted 21 pressures, good for 10th among interior defensive linemen.

Where this move could really help both players is allowing San Francisco to rotate more, as they now have another body in the defensive tackle room that can soak up a good number of snaps. This isn’t to say that the 49ers should cut Odighizuwa or Buckner’s snaps dramatically, but having them fresh for the playoffs should be the No. 1 priority.

With Buckner in the fold, the 49ers now have him, Odighizuwa, Gracen Halton, James Thompson Jr., and Sebastian Valdez as their top current defensive tackles. CJ West could also return at some point, but there was a clear need for a defensive tackle who could take some of the load off Odighizuwa and balance out the snaps more.

We also know that the 49ers will kick in some of their edges, such as Mykel Williams or Keion White, on passing downs, spreading out the snaps even more.

But San Francisco now has two quality pass rushers on the interior that can soak up snaps and keep each other fresh. The rotation also allows for the continued development of the team’s young defensive tackles and gives the team some much-needed depth up front. Good move all around, and there could be more coming in the front seven.

Defensively, the Browns decided man coverage was the best way to defend Pittsburgh and its offense. On 73% of Pittsburgh’s dropbacks, they faced man coverage.

Pittsburgh has faced man coverage on 42% of dropbacks, the highest rate through seven weeks since 2020, according to SumerSports. Pittsburgh finished with a 36% success rate against Cleveland’s man coverage, and the league average is 42%. The offense has posted an EPA/dropback of -0.19 against man coverage.

The bottom line is, the Steelers need man coverage beaters. Defenses will refuse to back off until the receivers prove they can defeat man-to-man independently. This is the matchup to watch on Sunday.

WR Notes: Zay Flowers was a low-end PPR WR1 even during Lamar Jackson’s three-game absence. With Jackson finally back in the saddle, Flowers can resume his quest for “poor man’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba” status. … Matthew Golden (shoulder, foot) appears genuinely questionable for Thursday evening’s game against the Panthers. Even if he goes, he could be a decoy/re-injury risk. His 2026 target totals are nevertheless the kind you must jam into lineups no matter what. … DJ Moore (shoulder) is poised to play for only the second time since September. Although the Bills received a few nice pop-up performances during Moore’s lengthy, stop-start absence, nothing changed the overall calculus. This remains an offense that badly needs Moore’s play-making and chain-moving ability. He’s an extreme re-injury risk but a must start for however long he manages to remain in the lineup this time around. … A.J. Brown is averaging 1.22 yards per route run through three 2026 appearances, ranking 66th amongst qualified wideouts. So, uhh, that could be better. The same isn’t really true of his usage since his return. He has commanded 16 targets on 64 Drake Maye attempts. That 25 percent target share would rank 12th on the season. For now, the Pats are still jamming Brown the ball. It is time for him to start rewarding their efforts.

The good news: Garrett Wilson confirmed he has not requested a trade. The bad news: Garrett Wilson had to confirm he has not requested a trade. Wilson has become an “it’s always something” player. His latest something is Omar Cooper Jr.’s cannon-shot return to the lineup over the past two weeks. Cooper is looking every bit his first-round pedigree. Wilson, meanwhile has been held under 50 yards three of the past four weeks. The exception was a Week 5 eruption spot against the Browns. Although Week 8 opponent Las Vegas is weaker on the ground than through the air, it is still very weak through the air. This is a get-right setup for New York’s cranky No. 1 wideout. … As for Cooper, you simply have to start him even if a let-down seems inevitable. The rookie banished a returning Adonai Mitchell to the shadow realm in Week 7. Having sufficiently demonstrated his upside, we can worry about Cooper’s potential downside later. … Luther Burden III is quietly 12th in target share at 21 percent. He has caught fewer than four passes one time all season and has been surging since Caleb Williams’ return. The Seahawks are as tough as opposing pass defenses get, but Burden is a summer hype all star who has earned his weekly spot in starting lineups.

He might be red lining the engine in the process, but Jameson Williams has been getting home as a strong fantasy option over the past three weeks. Now, he still isn’t commanding enough targets. He’s also not going to keep scoring four touchdowns for every seven catches. He feels risky in a spot like this weekend’s Vikings date, but the past three games are a reminder that for all the ever-present JaMo risk, there does indeed remain potential reward. … At long last, Emeka Egbuka has his quarterback back. Is that a good thing? Egbuka and Baker Mayfield weren’t exactly making beautiful music together earlier this season. The hope is that with a maturing rushing attack and settled-down defense, the Bucs' overall environment is better and the No. 1 wideout can finally get down to the needed business of scoring some fantasy points. … Carnell Tate has to be pretty damn good to be posting this consistent of returns with Cam Ward under center. Of course, scoring a touchdown has been a bit like drawing blood from a stone. You simply have to keep the faith that someone doing 5/70 on the reg will start finding the end zone with greater frequency even if it’s Ward under center.

It’s not an exaggeration to say Tre Tucker has been one of the WR2s to most consistently pair floor with upside. It feels like it can’t last, but that has been true for weeks now. Maybe it’s time to face the truth that Tucker needs to be in your lineup on a weekly basis. … Ladd McConkey (concussion) is back and presumably somewhat healthy after a disastrous, injury-marred first six games to the season. The Bolts had the bye week to ponder their sins. Post-bye is when bad clubs tend to circle the wagons around their best players. McConkey is the only player in the Chargers’ skill corps. He gets a fantasy do-over on the WR2/3 borderline. … You should never stay too long at the Germie Bernard casino. Week 7 was probably a predictable bust. Just as predictable would be Bernard getting back on the WR3 track in Week 8. His short-area work has simply become too important to an immobilized Aaron Rodgers.

KC Concepcion’s consistently strong target shares finally produced a Week 7 breakout. Although Deshaun Watson’s average intended air yards are actually middle of the pack, it never really made sense that it was down-field threat Denzel Boston who got off to a better rookie fantasy start than Concepcion. Don’t be surprised if Concepcion’s big day proves to be enduring rather than a fluke. … Jaylen Waddle (chest) probably needs a week on the shelf, but that has been true multiple times during his career before he went on to play anyways. If he does, he’s a no-numbers 2026 option who will be at significantly less than full health vs. a tough defense. Aka, struggling to crack the WR3 ranks. … That wasn’t a breakout from Makai Lemon so much as the bare minimum. It will also be replicable for another soft Week 8 matchup in the Commanders, as neither DeVonta Smith (hamstring) nor Dontayvion Wicks (ankle) have resumed practicing. … Caleb Douglas and Ja’Kobi Lane both created Week 7 excuses to get them into your WR4/second FLEX spots. Fun. Also likely to be frustrating on a week-to-week basis. Lane at least has a point chasey Week 8 game environment in the Bills. Douglas will be more of a floor play against the Patriots.

RB Notes: With Javonte Williams coming off his best 2026 performance and the game total soaring skywards for Cowboys/Cardinals there’s never been a better time to “point chase” with Williams’ rank. I doubt I will have him in the top 10 terribly often going forward, but that is inarguably where he belongs this weekend. … Josh Jacobs was the RB8 in his Week 7 return.
