Not ideal, though he did revert to 20-plus touches in Week 7 after falling below the mark for the first time in four games in Week 6. I’m not really sure what Warren’s long-term ranking should be, though I also know he has done nothing to remove himself from “must start” status since Dowdle’s return.

Bhayshul Tuten briefly eclipsed 60 percent of the Jaguars’ snaps in Week 5 but saw that number return to 57.7 heading into the Jags’ bye. Hardly a disaster. Also not a harbinger of every-week RB1 status moving forward, especially since Chris Rodriguez’s 29.6 mark against the Texans was his highest since Week 1. Set for a Week 8 road paving of the Colts, Tuten could find himself alternating drives with his 1B caddie. … Ashton Jeanty is barely producing as a rusher. So thank goodness he is really revving up the free PPR points machine. As Establish The Run’s Mark Dankenbring helpfully points out, Jeanty is commanding a target on 29.2 percent of his routes. That’s an extremely strong mark for a running back, especially one who is ostensibly an every-down player and not a passing-game specialist. Now, maybe Jeanty is trending that direction, but for now he is a PPR-based RB2 who could become a whole lot more if he ever gets in gear between the tackles. … Although it was another disappointing performance, Chase Brown came out of the Bengals’ bye week to his second highest snap percentage of the season. His Week 5 timeshare with Samaje Perine thankfully did not carry over. Maybe the situation will remain up in the air moving forward but for now Brown remains a “take your medicine” RB2 because of his touchdown and high-value handles upside.

The Vikings did not want to give Aaron Jones Sr. so much work during Jordan Mason’s month-long absence but they had no choice. Now the reverse might be true with Sr.’s knee acting up again. Mason did at least survive 15 Week 7 handles without incident. If Sr. indeed sits, Mason will be a must play in every format of fantasy vs. the Lions’ leaky defense. Even if Sr. goes, Mason will find himself on the RB2/3 borderline. … The Patriots’ backfield remains in a sort of suspended animation. Rhamondre Stevenson can’t quite achieve true bell-cow status, and TreVeyon Henderson is stuck firmly in “change of pace” territory. Week 6 pop-up hero Corey Kiner was nowhere to be found in Week 7. With the Pats touchdown road favorites against the Dolphins, we will stick with Stevenson’s all-around game and coaching staff trust in the top 20. … Coming off bye, it will be Separation Sunday in the Chargers’ backfield. I’m expecting the past week of reflection to come to the same pre-season conclusion: Omarion Hampton is not a great back, but he’s the best one the Bolts have.

Breece Hall’s (quad) slow-motion return appears to have finally reached its destination. Hall’s marathon absence had the unfortunate distinction of proving this should probably be a two-man backfield, as Braelon Allen was amongst the league’s most productive runners over the past month, even in some poor game environments. Whether or not that actually happens is far from assured — see the Steelers immediately resuming their Rico Dowdle usage upon his recent return — but Hall cannot be returned to his previous high-end RB2 rank until we see how this shakes out in Jersey. … It’s not the best year to be an Eagles running back. Dameon Pierce is seemingly the 99th to end up on injured reserve. Although he is currently dealing with back and hamstring issues, Saquon Barkley is apparently the healthiest runner Philly has at the moment. His snaps and touches will undoubtedly be rationed in Washington, but he will see the ball enough to remain a solid RB2/FLEX play in most formats. … The next man up behind Barkley is seeimgly 49ers castoff Elijah Mitchell. He’s worth an add, but you would have to be hurting pretty bad to get him into a 12-team league lineup. Jaydon Blue is also finally on the 53-man roster.

Jeremiyah Love appears poised to return after missing the past two weeks with various ankle difficulties. Should you “trust” him? What is trust, anyways? Should you concoct a far-fetched upside case for him? Now we’re talking. Love still has all the talent in the world, and the bookmakers are projecting all the points in the world for Cowboys/Cardinals. … Zach Charbonnet’s (knee) expected Week 7 return ended up being an okie doke, but his 2026 debut looks for real this time. Charbonnet’s role — RB3/FLEX who verges on RB2 nuisance — will probably remain the same as it was in 2025. The question is whether Emanuel Wilson holds onto his “poor man’s Kenneth Walker” role. At least for one week, we will assume that’s the case. With Charbonnet also looking likely to need an on-field ramp-up period, I will give a modest rankings advantage to Wilson. … Active for the first time since his NFL debut in Week 1, Jonah Coleman had the best overall role in the Broncos’ backfield in his Week 7 return. “Momentum” is only ever as good as the next Sunday for a Sean Payton running back, but it is certainly notable the head coach picked up where he left off with his rookie back in the opener. He’s a low-floor FLEX, but Coleman is the Broncos back to start if you must.

QB Notes: It’s been a while since we’ve had a national nightmare as long as Lamar Jackson’s absence with an ankle issue. Stop us if you have heard this one before, but it supposedly ends now. It couldn’t come at a better time for the Ravens or fantasy managers, as Jackson’s return arrives in time for a measuring stick matchup with the Bills. The game total is well north of 50, and the Bills’ defense has been anything but impressive. Despite the lingering question marks and bad taste, you return Jackson to your starting lineup without hesitation. … Although the Commanders’ bye week was mixed in, Jayden Daniels is the QB4 by average fantasy points since returning in Week 5. The production has felt somewhat fragile, but it has involved a big day both on the ground and through the air. He’s looking like the quarterback you thought you were drafting, while the same is very much not true of the Eagles defense Daniels is facing at home. … Dak Prescott finally had a multi-score start in the month of October. He was facing an Eagles defense that seems to be giving up on the season, though the Cardinals’ defense never even really started. Only the Bears are permitting more yards per opposing pass attempt than Arizona’s 8.5.

Trevor Lawrence had his best back-to-back starts of the year heading into the Jaguars’ Week 7 bye. He comes off the open date as a monstrous home favorite against the tanking Colts. Perhaps the Jags will try to get really established on the ground, but “the matchup is too easy” is never a good reason to pivot off a QB1. … Matthew Stafford has thrown for multiple touchdowns in 5-of-7 games, including three straight. The Chargers’ defense isn’t bad despite the team’s 0-6 start, but is slightly more vulnerable through the air than on the ground. Translation, Stafford is perfectly positioned for what is becoming his standard low-end QB1 outing. … Jared Goff has by far the most touchdown passes (14) of a quarterback who has yet to be intercepted. Our Jared is all grown up. It will be put to the test against a Vikings defense tied for fourth in picks (seven) and tied for first in sacks (21). This, even though Brian Flores’ unit has already had its bye. We almost never even worry about Goff at home, let alone bench him. But you are permitted a bit of Week 8 concern.

Caleb Williams has looked like an MVP contender with the major exception of Week 2 against the Vikings. That was at home. Now he must head on the road vs. the only defense to allow fewer aerial tallies than Minnesota, Seattle. Stunningly, the Seahawks are coughing up just 5.2 yards per attempt, 0.8 fewer than the next best unit, the Rams. Despite Williams’ stellar play and coach Ben Johnson’s creativity, this is a matchup to be feared. … Bryce Young is coming off his worst start of the season to a short-week road date with a Packers defense that quietly has as many interceptions (nine) as touchdowns allowed. Green Bay is one of only five Ds surrendering a QB rating below 80.0. Shootout conditions could still develop and help Young to a QB1 day, but he is a borderline option rather than set-and-forget starter. … Kyler Murray has completed four starts. He has three total touchdowns. He needs a big day in the worst way against a Lions defense that is not amongst the league’s best but has improved on its horrendous September form. Between his legs and above-average weapons, Murray has to spike a week at some point in the near future.

The good news: Kirk Cousins is getting votes of confidence from the Raiders’ coaching staff. The bad news … Kirk Cousins is getting votes of confidence from the Raiders’ coaching staff. The end is nigh. The Jets’ defense is mediocre enough that is is unlikely to be Week 8. … The end also appears nigh for Jacoby Brissett, though unlike Cousins, he doesn’t have a ready-made heir apparent waiting in the wings. Third-round rookie Carson Beck has been battling back issues of late. That means Brissett should be cleared for 60 minutes of ball against the Cowboys’ highly-unimpressive defense. … I’m just not sure what Patrick Mahomes is supposed to do. This is the worst collection of receiving talent in the league when Rashee Rice is on the shelf, and it’s not a whole lot better even when Rice plays. It makes Mahomes vulnerable to tough matchups, and the Broncos are another one for Week 8. … Baker Mayfield made his first start in a month and attempted only 11 passes. That will not be happening again, to put it mildly, but his status as a QB2 play vs. the Falcons’ good but far from great pass defense will depend on Emeka Egbuka’s (foot) health.

Micheal Penix Jr. has cracked the top 10 in EPA per play. He’s also top 10 in yards per attempt and top five in touchdown percentage. He is playing exceptionally well. It’s nevertheless not translating to elite fantasy play because of his limited overall volume. With the Bucs defense quietly playing quite well, Penix does not have an overly appealing Week 8 streamer spot. … Malik Willis is finally cutting loose on the ground just as his young skill corps gets healthy. It makes the QB2 streamer vision much easier to see, even for tough dates like Sunday’s showdown with the Patriots. … Cam Ward had his best overall start of the year against the Browns. It resulted in a QB26 finish. That was step one. He still needs to complete steps 2-9 before putting himself in the streamer mix. … The QB1 dream died long ago for Justin Herbert. The question coming out of the Chargers’ bye week is if he can even push for streamer value. He won’t against the Rams’ tough defense, but what changes the Bolts made during their bye will determine if Herbert is someone who can even be mentioned in this column.

item.title: Patrick Mahomes downplays past beef after Chiefs sign kicker Justin Tucker
item.description: Patrick Mahomes reflected on his conflict with Justin Tucker in the 2024 AFC championship after the Chiefs signed the veteran kicker.
item.content:encoded:
Before they were teammates on the Kansas City Chiefs, Patrick Mahomes and Justin Tucker went viral for butting heads ahead of the AFC championship game in 2024. They've since let bygones be bygones.

Back in January 2024, Mahomes and Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce took umbrage with where Tucker – then with the Baltimore Ravens – had decided to do his pregame kicking warmups. After the Chiefs signed Tucker on Wednesday, Oct. 28, Mahomes told reporters that he had moved on from the incident.

"We haven't had a lot of conversations ... but it wasn't like we ever had any beef or anything like that," Mahomes said. "I think at that moment, it was just competitors being competitors."

Mahomes said he understood that Tucker – "a big-time kicker for a long time" – was also trying to compete and help the Ravens earn a Super Bowl appearance at the time.

JUSTIN TUCKER: Chiefs sign disgraced former Ravens kicker to challenge Harrison Butker

Patrick Mahomes reacts to the #Chiefs signing K Justin Tucker to the practice squad. https://t.co/wdY25zbZl3

— Sports Radio 810 WHB (@SportsRadio810) October 28, 2026

"That stuff happened, but then you move on from that. At the end of the day we're just playing a game, and you want to compete and you want to win, but it wasn't like we had some longstanding beef that carried over after that game."

According to Kelce at the time, Tucker had broken an "unwritten rule" of setting up his kicking materials – a tee and kicking balls – in the Chiefs' designated area.

The Chiefs' stars responded in kind. Kelce threw Tucker's helmet and kicking balls to the side, and Mahomes kicked Tucker's tee away while progressing through his throwing warmup routine.

The Chiefs went on to win that AFC championship game and the Super Bowl that followed.

After the AFC championship game, Tucker said he saw all of the back-and-forth as "gamesmanship ... But it seemed to be taken a little more seriously.

"I'm totally willing to let it all go."

Tucker played one more season with the Ravens before the team released him in May 2025 amid an NFL investigation into accusations from 16 massage therapists of inappropriate sexual behavior. In June 2025, the league suspended Tucker 10 games to begin the season for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy.

The placekicker denied the allegations but did not appeal the NFL's decision. He served his suspension last year without an active contract.

Mahomes did not have an outsized reaction to the Chiefs' decision to sign the former Ravens kicker, saying the regularity of roster churn has numbed him to players additions.

"I try not to get too high or too low on anything," Mahomes said. "But I know (Chiefs GM Brett) Veach and them do a great job of bringing great players in, but for me it's about the Denver Broncos and moving on and continuing to get better. We have a lot of stuff that we have to clean up."

item.title: NFL Thursday Night Football preview: Panthers and Packers try to rebound from frustrating losses
item.description: The Panthers and Packers are both at or hovering around .500 coming into Thursday night.
item.content:encoded:
Is it worse to lose a close, heartbreaking game at the end, or be completely blown out? We could poll the Green Bay Packers and Carolina Panthers.

The two teams facing off this Thursday night are coming off losses, and those losses were much different. The Packers lost 20-17 to the Lions last week, with many miscues, including a partially blocked field goal late in the game that would have tied it. Fans and players alike also had a lot of issues with the officiating.

While the Packers could look back at a play or two that might have turned the game, the Panthers were done by halftime. They trailed the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 33-6 at halftime and lost 43-13 in a stunning blowout. The Panthers had looked like an improved team before whatever happened against the Buccaneers last week.

The Packers have had a strange season. They were not good for four weeks but escaped it with a 2-2 record. Then they blasted the Cowboys and Bears in back-to-back weeks before falling short against the Lions, though that's not a bad loss. The Panthers were 3-2 before the Buccaneers game with Bryce Young having a true breakout season. Young didn't play well against Tampa Bay but nobody on Carolina's side did. They have to show that performance was an anomaly, though they also had a loss to the Bears in which they gave up 59 points.

It's never a fun week for an NFL team after a loss. The best thing is to come back and play again right away. Both teams this Thursday are more appreciative than normal for the short week.

Who needs it more?

The difference between the situation for these two teams could be as easy as this: The Panthers play in the mediocre NFC South, and the Packers play in the NFC North which might be the NFL's toughest division. The Panthers don't want to take on another loss and fall behind .500, but there's not another team that will run away with that division. The Packers are already three losses behind the Vikings in the division and the Bears and Lions are very tough, too. Green Bay can't fall too far behind in the division, especially with a home loss against an opponent it is favored to beat.

Key player: Packers RB Josh Jacobs

The Packers will have a lot more balance with Jacobs off the commissioner's exempt list. Jacobs wasn't efficient in his return last week with just 36 rushing yards on 11 attempts, but he did add 55 yards and a touchdown on five catches. The Packers game was going nowhere without him in the lineup. While offensive line issues will continue to keep Green Bay from having a great running game, at least it should keep defenses honest. There should be some concern over how Jacobs plays on a short week, after not playing at all for the first six weeks. But he's facing a Panthers defense that gave up 258 rushing yards last week against the Buccaneers. Carolina's defense gave up 291 rushing yards in Week 1 to the Bears and while the run defense had improved after that, Sunday's performance against Tampa Bay was troubling. Jacobs and the Packers will be testing that run defense early on.

Betting market watch

This game was Packers -7 in the offseason, but has re-opened a combination of Green Bay -3.5 and -4 at sportsbooks — partially due to the fact that Carolina played one of the worst games of the season in a 43-13 loss as a 3-point home favorite against the Bucs. Keep an eye on WR Matthew Golden and DT Devonte Wyatt for the Packers, both of whom are questionable to play. The Panthers are a remarkable 13-0 ATS in their past 13 games after a loss. It's hard for Carolina to play any worse than last week, so was that a bad game or a bad sign? I think it was more likely a momentary breakdown and that Bryce Young & Co. can hang with a banged-up Green Bay team and keep this within the number. — Ben Fawkes

Check out more of Ben's work at the Yahoo Sports betting hub.

Fantasy football storylines

Fantasy managers are optimistic for Week 8's opener between the Panthers and Packers, as the total is set for 47.5. Here are three themes to consider as you enjoy the game.

1. Can Bryce Young get his groove back? Every time it feels like Young has fully entered the Circle of Trust, he seems to have a setback — Tampa Bay ate his lunch last week. The Green Bay defense has been better than expected this year, especially against the pass.

2. What does Josh Jacobs do for an encore? Jacobs checked in with a solid RB11 finish in his season debut, though it was the receiving game where he made his mark. Running lanes might be harder to find behind a Green Bay offensive line that's played poorly.

3. How will the Carolina WR room play out? Although Jalen Coker was undrafted while Tetairoa McMillan was a first round pick, the two players have produced at similar levels when both are on the field. Of course for either to hit his projection here, Young has to play better and the Carolina offensive line has to rebound from a messy game. — Scott Pianowski

item.title: The Number Crunch: Lack of separation hurting A.J. Brown
item.description: Inside some numbers from the Patriots’ loss to the Bears.
item.content:encoded:
Their first Thursday Night Football game of 2026 did not go as the Patriots had hoped. While the offense mostly did its part, New England allowed 30 or more points for the second time all season.

Let’s take a look at what held them from coming out victorious at Soldier Field.

A.J. Brown’s struggles

The Patriots are still awaiting the explosion of the receiver that they paid the hefty price of a 2028 first-round pick for. Brown, 29, played in his second game since his return from a high ankle sprain, which kept him out for four weeks. Speculation that this injury is still lingering is the hopeful view for New England. Out of the 61 receivers in Week 7 (min. 5 targets), Brown ranked the fourth-worst in average separation (SEP) at 1.5 yards. This battle to get open is now an ongoing issue for Brown, as he ranked seventh-worst out of 120 receivers in SEP last year (min. 45 targets).

It’s safe to say the lack of separation is leading to him not getting the action that he’s been used to in his illustrious career. Brown has three receptions in each of his three games this seas0n. In 2025, he only had four games in which he didn’t receive the ball at least three times.

It hasn’t taken him this long to have four or more receptions to start off a season since his rookie year. While it is a new team for Brown, and coming off an injury sustained in Week 1, it is fair to have concerns about what he will give the Patriots in terms of production this year, and the rest of his tenure in New England.

Turnover battle

There was only one turnover between the Patriots and Bears in Chicago. But that turnover was the first interception thrown by Drake Maye since Week 4 at Buffalo. It was costly one too. Following a scramble for a pickup of 15 yards, Maye launched his league-leading third red-zone interception. Since the game ended up being a one-score contest at 30-24, that underthrown ball intended for Eli Raridon may have decided the outcome.

While the offensive side for New England was mostly productive, the same could be said for Chicago. This marked the second game this season where the Bears committed no turnovers, and they are now 2-0 in this instance. Conversely, it was also the first game since Week 1 where New England did not force a turnover on defense, making them 0-2 when they can’t induce a mistake.

Lack of possession

While the Patriots offense was efficient, the unit didn’t have the ball enough to make the Bears uncomfortable. The Patriots had a season-low 54 snaps on offense, and a season-high 69 defensive snaps to go along with it. It made it even tougher for the Patriots to overcome defeat when the Bears offense dominated the fourth quarter in particular. Chicago had double the amount of plays as New England (26 to 13), and possessed the football at a whopping 12:21 minutes, to the 2:39 minutes that the Patriots had it.

This could be contributed to the complete lack of a rushing attack that the Patriots had. Maye was their leading rusher with 26 yards, beating out the three other running backs on the game day roster. New England carried the ball 17 times to the Bears’ 30 rushes. D’Andre Swift himself had 22 carries for 78 yards, along with a touchdown.

Drake Maye vs. Caleb Williams did not disappoint. Although this wasn’t the first matchup between the two top three picks in the 2024 NFL Draft, it was the first head-to-head since the definitive breakouts of both quarterbacks. While each of them played up to their capabilities, Williams ultimately got the best of Maye in primetime.

item.title: Bears acquire Jeffery Simmons ahead of Week 8 matchup with Seahawks
item.description: Jeffery Simmons will be in line to make his Bears debut in Seattle.
item.content:encoded:
An already strong test for the Seattle Seahawks in Week 8 just got a little tougher.

Ahead of their Monday Night Football trip to Seattle, the Chicago Bears made a major pre-trade deadline splash, acquiring All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported on Thursday.

In exchange for the 29-year-old Simmons, the Titans are receiving 2027 and 2028 first round picks, as well as a fourth round pick in ’27, while sending a ’28 fifth round pick back to Chicago.

Fresh off a career-best 11 sacks in 2025, Simmons and the Titans agreed to a three-year, $105.8 million extension over the summer. In seven games this year, he has totaled four sacks and six tackles for loss on a struggling team. Across 106 games in Tennessee, Simmons posted 46.5 sacks and 72 tackles for loss while making three All-Pro teams and four Pro Bowls.

Now, Simmons will join a high-flying Bears team that looks like a bona fide threat in the NFC, provided they can get even average play out of their defense — and the biggest splash of the Ben Johnson era will be a massive boost in that regard.

The trade comes just days before Chicago takes on the Seahawks in primetime, and days after the defending Super Bowl champs made a splash of their own. Now, in Quenton Nelson’s debut, he’ll have an immediate chance to prove his value to a contender as he lines up across from one of the league’s best defensive tackles — and a player he knows well from years battling in the AFC South.

(H/T letshide for putting this on The Feed first!)
